prompt: What does an AlloyDB primary write to the storage layer?
hint: Think of what makes a commit durable.

choices.text: Log records only
choices.why: Right. The log processing service builds the data blocks from them.

choices.text: Data pages, after each checkpoint
choices.why: That is a PostgreSQL server on its own disk; AlloyDB's primary writes no pages.

choices.text: Both the log and the pages, to a disk in its own zone
choices.why: The primary owns no disk; the storage is regional and shared.

choices.text: Whole rows, which the read pool then indexes
choices.why: Nothing is indexed by the read pool; it reads the same blocks the primary does.

prompt: Quitanda adds a third node to its AlloyDB read pool. What happens to the storage line of the bill?

choices.text: It grows by the size of the database, for the new copy
choices.why: That is a Cloud SQL replica, which keeps a full copy of its own.

choices.text: It grows by the new node's cache
choices.why: The cache is part of the node's machine, billed as vCPUs and memory, not storage.

choices.text: Nothing; the cluster's storage is billed once
choices.why: Right. The pricing page says storage costs do not change when read nodes are added.

choices.text: It doubles, because reads are billed per GiB scanned
choices.why: AlloyDB has no charge per read or per GiB scanned.

prompt: Quitanda's write load grows beyond what the largest AlloyDB machine can absorb, while reads stay flat. What is the next step?
hint: Count the writers in a cluster.

choices.text: Add read pool nodes until the writes fit
choices.why: Read nodes take only reads; every write still goes through the one primary.

choices.text: Spread writes over many machines, as Spanner does
choices.why: Right. AlloyDB has exactly one writer, and that is the line where Spanner begins.

choices.text: Turn on the columnar engine on the primary
choices.why: The columnar engine speeds up analytical reads and adds work to writes.

choices.text: Add a second primary in another zone
choices.why: A regional primary's second node is a standby that serves nothing until a failover.

prompt: Why does a remote storage layer not make every AlloyDB query slower?
hint: Count the places a page can be found before the storage service.

choices.text: Two caches per node: memory and local storage
choices.why: Right. The storage service is reached only when both miss.

choices.text: The storage layer is in the same machine as the primary
choices.why: It is a regional service, spread over the zones, outside the nodes.

choices.text: Queries are answered from the log, never from pages
choices.why: Queries read pages; the log is what the pages are built from.

choices.text: Read pool nodes copy the whole database at start-up
choices.why: Read nodes hold no copy; they read blocks on demand.

prompt: Which `--availability-type` gives an AlloyDB primary a standby in another zone?
hint: The other value is one zone.

choices.text: `ZONAL`
choices.why: One node in one zone, with no automatic failover.

choices.text: `REGIONAL`
choices.why: Right. Two nodes in two zones, both billed.

choices.text: `READ_POOL`
choices.why: That is a value of `--instance-type`, for an instance that takes only reads.

choices.text: `MULTI_REGIONAL`
choices.why: No such value; a copy in another region is a secondary cluster.

prompt: With `--cpu-count=16` and no machine type, how many GiB of memory does an AlloyDB node have?
Quitanda wants its read pool to survive the loss of one zone. What is the smallest pool that can?
hint: The help says what a pool of one can be.

choices.text: One node, regional
choices.why: A read pool of size 1 can only be zonal.

choices.text: Two nodes, placed in two zones
choices.why: Right. A pool of two or more nodes spreads them over zones.

choices.text: Three nodes, one per zone, which is the minimum for a quorum
choices.why: There is no quorum among read nodes; two is enough to span zones.

choices.text: Any size, because the storage layer is regional
choices.why: The storage survives a zone; a node in the lost zone does not.

prompt: On the plain PostgreSQL of this lesson, why did October's revenue by district read every page of `orders`?

choices.text: The filter on `day` was applied after the aggregate
choices.why: The filter ran in the scan, and removed rows rather than pages.

choices.text: Whole rows are read, and October's are everywhere
choices.why: Right. Every page has to be opened to find them, address and notes included.

choices.text: `SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0` disables indexes
choices.why: It keeps the query to one process; there was no index on `day` to use.

choices.text: The columnar engine was off
choices.why: There is no columnar engine on plain PostgreSQL at all.

prompt: Which Quitanda query gains least from AlloyDB's columnar engine?
hint: Many rows and few columns is its shape.

choices.text: Revenue by district for the whole year
choices.why: Many rows, three columns: exactly what it is for.

choices.text: The number of cancelled orders per month
choices.why: Many rows, two columns.

choices.text: One customer's order by its primary key, every column
choices.why: Right. One row by its index is what a row store already does in a handful of buffers.

choices.text: The average total of orders delivered to Mooca
choices.why: Many rows, three columns.

prompt: The full table was 51,658 pages and the three-column table 11,840. How many times fewer pages did the narrow scan read? One decimal place.
hint: Divide the larger by the smaller.

prompt: Quitanda turns on the columnar engine only on the analysts' read pool. What does that buy?

choices.text: The checkout's primary never gives memory to a column store
choices.why: Right. The column store competes for memory, so it lives where the reports run.

choices.text: The column store stops costing anything
choices.why: Its memory is the pool's memory, billed with the nodes.

choices.text: The primary's writes stop reaching the column store
choices.why: Changes reach the column store wherever it lives; AlloyDB keeps it up to date.

choices.text: Reports may now use `google_columnar_engine_add` on PostgreSQL
choices.why: The function exists only on AlloyDB.

prompt: What changes in an application that moves from Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL to AlloyDB?

choices.text: The schema, because primary keys decide placement
choices.why: That is Spanner, whose keys decide where rows live.

choices.text: The connection string
choices.why: Right. AlloyDB is PostgreSQL; the move is the closest of the steps.

choices.text: Every query, to the GoogleSQL dialect
choices.why: AlloyDB speaks PostgreSQL; GoogleSQL is one of Spanner's dialects.

choices.text: The driver, for a proprietary protocol
choices.why: AlloyDB uses PostgreSQL's drivers and protocol.

prompt: Why does this lab practise on plain PostgreSQL rather than AlloyDB Omni?
hint: What is Omni missing that the lesson is about?

choices.text: Omni is not published for Linux
choices.why: Google publishes it as a container image for Linux, Docker and Kubernetes.

choices.text: Omni has no columnar engine, which is what this lesson measures
choices.why: The columnar engine is inside Omni.

choices.text: Omni keeps data on its own disks, with no shared storage
choices.why: Right. The part that sets AlloyDB apart is the part Omni leaves out.

choices.text: Omni needs an AlloyDB cluster to connect to
choices.why: Omni runs on its own, with no cluster behind it.

prompt: Match each product to how its reads grow.
hint: One of them grows writes the same way.

pairs.right: Read replicas, each with a full copy
Read pool nodes reading one shared storage
More nodes, which serve reads and writes by key range

prompt: Which of these is NOT a line on an AlloyDB bill?

choices.text: vCPUs and memory of every node
choices.why: Billed per vCPU-hour and per GiB-hour.

choices.text: Storage the cluster holds
choices.why: Billed per GiB-month of what is used.

choices.text: I/O requests to the storage layer
choices.why: Right. AlloyDB has no charge per read or per write.

choices.text: Backup storage
choices.why: Billed per GiB-month at the backup rate.

prompt: At São Paulo's list prices, what does one AlloyDB node of 8 vCPUs and 64 GiB cost for 730 hours, in USD to the cent?
Quitanda's shape grows from two read machines to four, on both products, with the data unchanged. What happens to the amount of data at which AlloyDB's bill meets Cloud SQL's?
hint: Each reader adds compute on both sides, and a disk on one.

choices.text: It stays at about 4,370 GiB, because the line depends on how much data there is and on nothing else
choices.why: The line is a compute difference over a storage difference per GiB, and both move.

choices.text: It falls, to about 3,380 GiB
choices.why: Right. Each reader widens the compute gap by about 593 a month, and adds 0.255 a GiB to Cloud SQL's storage: (6 × 1,445.87 − 1,704.70 − 4 × 852.64) / (1.53 − 0.476909).

choices.text: It rises, because each AlloyDB read node costs about 593 a month more than a replica
choices.why: It does, but each replica also brings a full disk, and past about 2,330 GiB that disk costs more than the 593.

choices.text: It cannot be computed without a free trial
choices.why: It is arithmetic on the pricing pages, like the 4,370.

prompt: Put the steps of building Quitanda's AlloyDB orders database in order.
hint: The cluster owns the storage before any machine exists.
items: `gcloud alloydb clusters create`, with the network and continuous backup
A `READ_POOL` of two nodes for the shop
The columnar engine flag on a second read pool for the analysts

prompt: Which of these follow from AlloyDB's shared storage layer? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of what a read node no longer needs.

choices.text: A read node adds no storage to the bill
choices.why: Yes; there is one storage layer per cluster.

choices.text: A new read node has no copy to build before it serves
choices.why: Yes; it reads the blocks that are already there.

choices.text: Storage is billed by what is used rather than by a size chosen in advance
choices.why: Yes; the storage scales up and down by itself.

choices.text: Writes can go to any node of a read pool
choices.why: Every write goes through the one primary.

choices.text: A `DELETE` without a `WHERE` can be undone from a read node
choices.why: The read node reads the same storage and sees the delete at once; continuous backup undoes it.

prompt: AlloyDB keeps the log for a recovery window, so a cluster can be restored to any moment inside it. That feature is continuous ___.
